title: Realtime
readme:
Phase 26 - Realtime

This package teaches Supabase Realtime as an optional freshness layer for TaskFlow.
The production direction uses database-triggered private Broadcast events scoped by Workspace Membership, then TanStack Query invalidation/refetch on clients.

The reference snapshot is illustrative and should be reconciled with the exact TaskFlow repository before copy/paste.

lessons.body:
Realtime Mental Model and When It
Earns Its Place
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

The problem Realtime solves
• User A changes a Task while User B is looking at the same Workspace.

• Without Realtime, User B sees the change only after manual refresh, navigation, focus refetch, or
polling.

• Realtime reduces the time between committed server truth and another client learning that it
changed.

Do not confuse freshness with authority
The event does not become the database. The browser uses the event as a hint that cached server
state may now be stale. HTTP/API reads still reconstruct authoritative state.

When Realtime earns its cost
• Collaborative task boards where changes from coworkers should appear quickly.

• Live operations consoles where stale state has real workflow cost.

• Notifications or activity streams where delay matters.

• Presence/typing/cursor indicators for collaborative experiences.

When normal refetch is enough
• Rarely changed settings pages.

• Forms mostly edited by one person.

• Admin reports where refresh every 30-60 seconds is acceptable.

• Screens where realtime complexity would exceed UX value.

Decision rule
Start with HTTP + TanStack Query. Add Realtime only to flows where stale data is an actual product
problem.

Broadcast, Presence and Postgres
Changes
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Three capabilities
Three Realtime capabilities - three different jobs

Broadcast                            Postgres Changes                             Presence

Low-latency app/database events               Direct row-change stream            Ephemeral online/activity state
Recommended for scalable DB changes                   Simpler setup                          Who is here?
Private channel authorization          Less scalable under many subscribers        Not durable business data

TaskFlow choice: Broadcast for persistent Task changes; Presence only for future ephemeral collaboration.

Broadcast
Broadcast sends low-latency messages to channel subscribers. For database changes, Supabase
recommends Broadcast as the scalable and secure approach, typically emitted by a database trigger
using realtime.broadcast_changes().

Postgres Changes
Postgres Changes streams table changes directly and is easy to start with. Its authorization/scaling
model becomes more expensive as subscriber counts grow because changes may need
per-subscriber access checks.

Presence
Presence synchronizes ephemeral connected-client state such as “online”, “viewing this board”, or
cursor metadata. It is not a durable source of business truth.

TaskFlow decision
Persistent Task                   Use database-triggered private Broadcast.
changes

Prototype / simple                Postgres Changes is acceptable for learning or small use cases.
low-scale CDC

Who is online?                    Presence, if/when TaskFlow develops a real collaboration requirement.

TaskFlow Broadcast Architecture
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

End-to-end path
TaskFlow Realtime data path

User A                 NestJS                    Postgres      DB trigger          Realtime
mutation              rules + auth                commit        broadcast              WebSocket

User B browser                TanStack Query
private channel               invalidate/refetch

Realtime is a freshness signal. NestJS + PostgreSQL remain authoritative.

Why the event begins after commit
The Task write still goes through NestJS, authorization, business rules, Repository/Prisma and
PostgreSQL. A Postgres AFTER trigger emits an event only when the database change actually
happens.

Topic granularity
TaskFlow uses one private topic per Workspace Task stream: workspace:<workspaceId>:tasks. This
avoids one channel per Task while still keeping tenant boundaries explicit.

Why the browser subscribes directly to Supabase
Realtime
NestJS remains the write/API authority, but the WebSocket freshness path can go directly from
Supabase Realtime to the authenticated browser. We are not duplicating business logic in Realtime;
we are delivering change notifications.

Failure philosophy
If Realtime is unavailable, the app degrades to normal TanStack Query behavior: initial fetch,
invalidation from local mutations, focus/reconnect refetch, manual refresh. That is a healthy
architecture.

lessons.body:
Database Trigger and Workspace Topic
Design
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Trigger function
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.broadcast_task_changes()
RETURNS trigger
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = ''
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
project_id uuid;
workspace_id uuid;
BEGIN
project_id := CASE
WHEN TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN OLD."projectId"
ELSE NEW."projectId"
END;

SELECT p."workspaceId"
INTO workspace_id
FROM public."Project" p
WHERE p.id = project_id;

IF workspace_id IS NOT NULL THEN
PERFORM realtime.broadcast_changes(
'workspace:' || workspace_id::text || ':tasks',
TG_OP,
TG_OP,
TG_TABLE_NAME,
TG_TABLE_SCHEMA,
NEW,
OLD
);
END IF;

RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

Attach the trigger
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS task_realtime_broadcast
ON public."Task";

CREATE TRIGGER task_realtime_broadcast
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
ON public."Task"
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION public.broadcast_task_changes();

Why use an AFTER trigger
• The event describes a database change that has actually been accepted.

• The browser should not be notified about a write that later fails.

• The topic is derived from persisted Task -> Project -> Workspace relationships, not browser input.

Production note
If Workspace lookup becomes a hot path, measure it before denormalizing. A later schema could
store workspaceId directly on Task, but Phase 26 does not change the data model merely for
convenience.

lessons.body:
Private Channels and Realtime
Authorization
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Authorization path
Private workspace channel authorization

Supabase JWT                  Realtime join                  RLS policy             Membership

Topic: workspace:<workspaceId>:tasks

Policy allows SELECT on realtime.messages only when the JWT subject maps to a Workspace Membership.

This RLS protects the Realtime channel. NestJS still owns business authorization for writes.

Membership helper
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.can_receive_task_topic(
requested_topic text
)
RETURNS boolean
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = ''
AS $$
SELECT EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM public."Membership" m
JOIN public."User" u
ON u.id = m."userId"
WHERE u."authSubject" = (SELECT auth.uid())::text
AND requested_topic =
'workspace:' || m."workspaceId"::text || ':tasks'
);
$$;

Realtime SELECT policy
CREATE POLICY
"workspace members receive task broadcasts"
ON realtime.messages
FOR SELECT TO authenticated
USING (
realtime.messages.extension = 'broadcast'
AND public.can_receive_task_topic(
(SELECT realtime.topic())
)
);

Function permissions
The full reference migration revokes public execution and grants the helper only to the authenticated
role.

Important architectural distinction
This RLS authorizes the Realtime topic; NestJS still authorizes Task reads and writes.

Project setting

For production, disable public channel access and join with private: true so the Realtime policy is
enforced.

lessons.body:
TanStack Query Integration: Invalidate
First, Patch Selectively
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Default strategy
Realtime event + TanStack Query

Broadcast event                       Handler                     invalidateQueries                       API
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE               small + idempotent                   taskKeys.all                     refetch

Why invalidate first? The backend already owns authorization, filters, pagination and derived state.

Patch the cache directly only when the event contract is stable and the update is easy to prove correct.

Why invalidate is the safe default
• NestJS already owns authorization and business rules.

• Phase 15 already owns search, filters, sorting, pagination and metadata.

• Phase 25 already owns optimistic local UX for the current user.

• A Realtime event can simply mark cached Task data stale and let the API rebuild the correct view.

Targeted invalidation options
// Simple and safe:
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
queryKey: taskKeys.all,
})

// Narrower when the event contract gives a reliable Task id:
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
queryKey: taskKeys.detail(taskId),
})
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
queryKey: taskKeys.lists(),
})

When direct cache patching is justified
Patch with setQueryData only when the event schema is stable, the update is easy to prove correct,
and you are not rebuilding authorization/filter/pagination logic in the browser. Otherwise invalidate.

Burst events
A later optimization may debounce/coalesce invalidations for high-frequency streams. Start correct
first, then measure network churn before adding complexity.

lessons.body:
Realtime with Optimistic Updates
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

The same mutation can generate two signals
User A clicks DONE
-> optimistic UI predicts DONE
-> HTTP PATCH /tasks/:id
-> Postgres commits DONE
-> Broadcast event arrives
-> mutation response arrives
-> onSettled invalidates too

Is duplicate invalidation wrong?
Usually no. Invalidation is idempotent from the application point of view: both signals say “the cache
may be stale.” The cost is extra refetch work, not data corruption. Optimize only if measurements
show meaningful churn.

Do not suppress every self-originated event
Trying to perfectly identify “my own” database broadcast adds correlation state and can accidentally
ignore a server-side change you still need. TaskFlow first accepts harmless duplicate freshness
signals.

Conflict behavior
• If another user changes the Task while your optimistic mutation is pending, the server remains the
authority.

• Serial mutation scopes from Phase 25 still protect same-Task mutation order in the local client.

• Realtime invalidation helps surface remote commits quickly.

• A 409/403 response still rolls back the local optimistic prediction.

Rule
Optimistic UI improves perceived latency. Realtime improves cross-client freshness.
Neither becomes the source of truth.

lessons.body:
Multi-Tenant Workspace Channel
Strategy
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Topic design
workspace:<workspaceId>:tasks

Examples:
workspace:11111111-...:tasks
workspace:22222222-...:tasks

Why Workspace scope
• One channel can cover all Task changes visible within the current Workspace.

• Changing Workspace naturally tears down the old channel and joins the new one.

• The Realtime Authorization policy maps the JWT subject to TaskFlow Membership.

• The topic itself contains no secret; authorization decides whether the subscriber may receive it.

Avoid one global Task channel
A global tasks channel would force every tenant event through one topic and make tenant isolation
harder to reason about. Multi-tenant systems benefit from a topic boundary that mirrors authorization
scope.

Avoid one channel per row by default
A channel for every Task can create excessive joins and cleanup pressure. Use fine-grained topics
only when the interaction genuinely needs them, such as a deeply collaborative Task detail view.

Workspace switching
Workspace URL/context changes -> remove old Realtime channel -> set current auth -> join new
private channel -> invalidate Task queries after SUBSCRIBED.

Presence and Ephemeral Collaboration
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Presence is not Task persistence
Presence answers questions like “Who is viewing this board?” or “Who is online?” It should not
represent Task status, approvals, payroll totals, inventory quantities, or other durable business facts.

Possible future use
channel
.on('presence', { event: 'sync' }, () => {
const viewers = channel.presenceState()
// Render "3 people viewing this board"
})
.subscribe(async status => {
if (status === 'SUBSCRIBED') {
await channel.track({
userId,
displayName,
viewing: 'tasks-board',
onlineAt: new Date().toISOString(),
})
}
})

Good presence payloads
• display name/avatar reference

• current collaborative surface

• cursor/selection metadata if needed

• ephemeral online timestamp

Bad presence payloads
• access token

• sensitive HR/payroll data

• database truth that must survive disconnects

• large user profile objects

TaskFlow decision
Phase 26 teaches Presence but does not ship it as a required TaskFlow feature. We only add it later if
collaboration UX needs it.

lessons.body:
Reliability, Scaling and
Troubleshooting
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture

Realtime is lossy from the app perspective
Clients can sleep, lose Wi-Fi, change networks, suspend background tabs, or disconnect during token
expiry. Therefore TaskFlow never assumes it observed every event. Reconnect means: rejoin +
refetch authoritative state.

Subscription statuses
• SUBSCRIBED - channel is joined; refresh current data.

• CHANNEL_ERROR - inspect the full error payload.

• TIMED_OUT - connectivity/join problem.

• CLOSED - channel ended; determine whether expected cleanup or unexpected disconnect.

Built-in reconnection
The Realtime protocol/client supports reconnection with backoff. Application code should still make
recovery idempotent and refresh server state after re-subscription.

Scaling lesson
Supabase currently recommends Broadcast for database-change subscriptions because Postgres
Changes can become costly under many subscribers; each database change can require
authorization work across subscribers. Measure your own workload and plan limits.

Troubleshooting order
• Confirm the user has a valid Supabase session/JWT.

• Confirm setAuth() occurs before joining a private channel.

• Confirm topic string exactly matches the policy.

• Confirm Membership/authSubject mapping.

• Confirm Realtime public-access/private-channel setting.

• Confirm trigger exists and fires.

• Check Realtime logs and browser WebSocket frames.

• Confirm removeChannel cleanup to avoid duplicate subscriptions.

Observability
Log channel topic (not token), status, Workspace id, reconnect count, error category and request/user
correlation where policy allows. Never log access tokens.

• Take User B offline.

• Make a status change from User A with optimistic UI.

You can explain Broadcast vs Postgres Changes vs Presence, secure a private Workspace channel,

1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
database/event source -> Supabase Realtime channel -> authorized/scoped subscription -> event handler -> query cache reconcile -> UI

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Realtime

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 26 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Add realtime synchronization without creating a second source of truth or leaking unauthorized events.

Required artifact
Realtime task updates that merge into TanStack Query state with scoped subscriptions and reconnect behavior.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can scope subscriptions.
• Can reconcile realtime with server cache.
• Can recover after disconnect.
• Can explain presence/broadcast/database-change differences.

Independent build sequence
1. Choose the exact collaborative event that benefits from realtime rather than subscribing to everything.
2. Create a channel scoped to workspace/board context and define subscription lifecycle.
3. Feed events into query cache updates or invalidation instead of a parallel global store.
4. Deduplicate events that echo the current user's own mutation.
5. Test disconnect/reconnect and ensure a fresh server query repairs any missed events.
6. Verify authorization/data exposure boundaries for every subscription filter/channel.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 26: Realtime. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Acceptance criteria

Evidence packet

references.preview:
# Postgres Changes alternative

For a small prototype you can subscribe directly:

```ts
const channel = supabase
  .channel("task-postgres-changes")
  .on(
    "postgres_changes",
    {
      event: "*",
      schema: "public",
      table: "Task",
    },
    () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: taskKeys.all }),
  )
  .subscribe();
```

TaskFlow Phase 26 prefers Broadcast for database-change delivery because Supabase currently recommends Broadcast for scalability/security. Keep this alternative for comparison and troubleshooting, not as the production default.

# TaskFlow Phase 26 Realtime Snapshot

This reference implements Realtime as a freshness layer, not as a new backend.

- Writes still go Browser -> NestJS -> business rules -> repository -> PostgreSQL.
- PostgreSQL trigger emits private Supabase Broadcast events after Task changes.
- Browser subscribes to one private Workspace Task channel.
- Realtime Authorization checks existing TaskFlow Membership.
- Realtime events invalidate TanStack Query Task keys.
- Reconnect/subscription success triggers an authoritative refetch.
- No direct browser Task writes are introduced.

# Realtime Decision Table

| Need | Default |
|---|---|
| Coworker Task changes should appear quickly | Private Broadcast + query invalidation |
| Tiny prototype / simplest DB CDC | Postgres Changes |
| Who is online / viewing board | Presence |
| Rare settings changes | Normal query refetch only |
| Payroll finalization | HTTP mutation + explicit confirmation; Realtime only as notification |
| High-frequency cursor movement | Broadcast, not database persistence |

Realtime is optional. HTTP correctness must remain intact without it.

# Sources

- [Supabase - Subscribing to Database Changes](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/subscribing-to-database-changes) - Broadcast is the recommended database-change method for scalability and security; Postgres Changes is simpler but scales less well. Includes realtime.broadcast_changes trigger pattern.
- [Supabase - Realtime Authorization](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/authorization) - Private channels use RLS policies on realtime.messages; permissions are evaluated when the client joins a topic.
- [Supabase - Realtime Concepts](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/concepts) - Defines Channels, topics, Broadcast, Presence and Postgres Changes.
- [Supabase - Realtime Architecture](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/architecture) - Describes Broadcast from Postgres, WAL/replication behavior and Realtime internals.
- [Supabase - Broadcast](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/broadcast) - Documents database-triggered Broadcast, private channels, replay and broadcast payloads.
- [Supabase - Realtime Protocol](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/protocol) - Documents access-token refresh, server events, reconnection behavior and broadcast protocol.
- [Supabase JS - removeChannel](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/removechannel) - Documents explicit channel teardown and removal.
- [Supabase JS - setAuth](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/javascript/setauth) - Documents the JWT used for Realtime authorization and RLS.
- [Supabase - Realtime Limits](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/limits) - Documents connection/message limits and Postgres Changes scaling considerations.
- [TanStack Query - QueryClient](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/reference/QueryClient) - Provides invalidateQueries and setQueryData used to synchronize Realtime events with query cache.

-- Phase 26: broadcast committed Task changes to Workspace-scoped private topics.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.broadcast_task_changes()
RETURNS trigger
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = ''
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
  project_id uuid;
  workspace_id uuid;
BEGIN
  project_id := CASE
    WHEN TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN OLD."projectId"
    ELSE NEW."projectId"
  END;

  SELECT p."workspaceId"
  INTO workspace_id
  FROM public."Project" p

-- Phase 26: authorize private Workspace Task topics from TaskFlow membership.
-- This policy protects Realtime channel joins/reads. NestJS still authorizes API writes.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.can_receive_task_topic(
  requested_topic text
)
RETURNS boolean
LANGUAGE sql
STABLE
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = ''
AS $$
  SELECT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM public."Membership" m
    JOIN public."User" u
      ON u.id = m."userId"
    WHERE u."authSubject" = (SELECT auth.uid())::text
      AND requested_topic =
        'workspace:' || m."workspaceId"::text || ':tasks'

# Phase 26 Realtime Test Matrix

| Scenario | Expected |
|---|---|
| User A and B belong to same Workspace | Both can subscribe to private Task topic |
| User B does not belong to Workspace | User B cannot receive Workspace Task broadcasts |
| User A updates Task through NestJS | DB trigger emits UPDATE after commit |
| User B is online | Task query invalidates/refetches automatically |
| User B offline during several changes | Reconnect/SUBSCRIBED refetch catches current state |
| Local optimistic update succeeds | Realtime + mutation invalidations still converge to server truth |
| Local optimistic update gets 409 | Local rollback works; Realtime does not override business error semantics |
| Workspace switch | Old channel removed; new Workspace channel joined |
| Component unmount | removeChannel called |
| Bad topic / no membership | subscription denied / no data delivered |
| CHANNEL_ERROR or TIMED_OUT | full error logged without token |
| Realtime disabled | normal HTTP query/mutation flow still works |
